extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetic theory / advanced creative-writing readers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for choosing diction and employing metre in metrical (poetic) composition — when poetic language must differ from prose, how metre arises and what it demands of diction, figures, and unity. Useful for evaluating or composing serious metrical poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of metrical composition essentially different from that of prose
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be, and ought to be, an 'essential difference between the language of prose and metrical composition.' The question is not merely shared words but differences in construction, arrangement, and kinds/frequency of figures which make some expressions fit for one and not the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing poetry, distinguish mere overlap of words from deeper architectural differences in sentence-order, construction, and figurative use. Ask whether an arrangement of words that is natural in prose would be disproportionate, heterogeneous, or unfit in metrical poetry (and vice versa). Examples: Daniel’s 'prosaic' verse vs. genuinely poetical stanzas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre should be accompanied by the natural language of excitement
rubrics_metrics.description: As 'the elements of metre owe their existence to a state of increased excitement,' the metre itself should be accompanied by the natural language of excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metrical diction ought to reflect heightened feeling: expect intensified imagery, repetition, and animated phrasing that naturally arise from excitement rather than flat conversational tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traces of present volition must be discernible in metrical language
rubrics_metrics.description: Because metre is 'formed into metre artificially, by a voluntary act,' the metrical language should show the traces of present volition — conscious shaping and purpose — alongside spontaneous feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the poem shows both impulsive feeling and deliberate artistic control (e.g., careful selection/order of words, rhythmic shaping). A good metrical line balances spontaneity with evident craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union/interpenetration of passion and will
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be 'not only a partnership, but a union; an interpenetration of passion and of will, of spontaneous impulse and of voluntary purpose' in metrical poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for harmony between fervor and form: passion should supply material and energy while the will (art) organizes and tempers it for pleasurable effect. Expect more frequent figures and vivifying language because of this union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre stimulates attention and therefore requires appropriate matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre 'tends to increase the vivacity and susceptibility both of the general feelings and of the attention' by surprise and re-excitation; where appropriate material is not provided, the metre will disappoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use metre as decoration alone. The subject, thought, and diction must be commensurate with the heightened attention metre produces; otherwise the result feels empty or mismatched (a 'disappointment').

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency and kind of figures should suit metrical composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Because metre both arises from and maintains excitement, it 'tends to produce a more frequent employment of picturesque and vivifying language' and figures of speech than would be natural elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and accept a higher density of figurative language in poetry, including repetition (when genuinely illustrative of passion). But distinguish tasteful, pleasure-producing frequency from excessive or trivial ornament (e.g., over-reliance on low devices). The essay praises high-kind repetition (Deborah song) and warns against mere gimmicks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arbitrary, capricious, or illogical diction for novelty's sake
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet who 'uses an illogical diction, or a style fitted to excite only the low and changeable pleasure of wonder by means of groundless novelty, substitutes a language of folly and vanity' instead of natural feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject novelty that exists only to astonish. Evaluate whether unusual phrasing serves sense and emotion; if it's merely capricious or illogical, it's an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not indiscriminately adopt the 'real language of men' (rustic dialect) as poetic diction
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal to 'imitate, and, as far as is possible, to adopt the very language of men' (i.e., the rustic or low language) is impracticable: every man's language varies by knowledge and feeling; the order and organization of diction matter as much as the words themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet must possess and select language consciously; one cannot simply transfer a class-dialect wholesale into poetry. Assess whether purportedly 'real' rustic language has been adapted (omitting provincial peculiarities and re-ordering sentences) to meet poetic necessities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit provincialisms and accidental peculiarities before using rustic speech in poems
rubrics_metrics.description: The language of rustics 'varies in every county, nay in every village' and contains peculiarities that must be omitted or changed before it can serve a poem (except in drama or professed imitation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If rustic diction is used, check that provincialisms or erratic colloquialisms have been judiciously edited out or transformed so the verse attains generality and poetic fitness; otherwise the adoption is neither practical nor desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incongruous images and confused personification
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines such as 'And reddening Phoebus lifts his golden fire' are faulted for conveying incongruous images, conflating cause and effect, or confusing the real thing with a personified representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate figurative language for congruity and coherence. Mythological personification may be a historic poetic device, but it becomes faulty when it produces confused or incongruous imagery; judge such usages by sense and age-appropriateness (hackneyed images are accidental faults).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forcing colloquial/prosaic diction into rhyme or metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Inserting rhyme into sentences that are 'exclusively colloquial' produces a sense of oddity and strangeness; metre and colloquial order may clash (example: passages from 'The Sailor's Mother').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When setting naturally colloquial speech into metrical/rhymed form, ensure the diction and rhyme are congruent; otherwise the rhyme will feel forced and the effect uneasy. Reconsider diction or form where ordinary speech and metrical demands conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry must avoid being merely prosaic even when sense is weighty
rubrics_metrics.description: Verses can be 'prosaic'—i.e., their diction and order would find their appropriate place in prose—rendering them unpoetic even if their sense is weighty and interesting (example: many passages by Daniel labeled 'prosaic Daniel').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether lines, despite strong sense, possess a prose-like order or tone that makes them unsuitable to verse. Mark such passages as failures of poetic diction rather than of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition requires unity—assimilate all parts to the essential/important parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The human instinct seeks unity by harmonious adjustment; 'all the parts of an organized whole must be assimilated to the more important and essential parts.' Imitation (in poetry) consists in inter-fusing the same throughout the radically different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a poem on whether its parts harmonize and are adjusted to the central elements. Disparate tonal, figurative, or structural parts that do not assimilate to central purpose indicate faulty composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on metre's historic mnemonic/associative power alone to justify metrical form
rubrics_metrics.description: While metre historically aided recollection and preservation (oral tradition), this is not a sufficient reason for choosing metrical form; content, aptness, and diction must justify metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing, ask whether metre is necessary for the poem's effects or merely an inherited/ornamental form. If metre is not justified by content or diction, prose might better suit the material.
